title: Canada raises rates as firms signal that prolonged energy costs will reach customers
summary: The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.50% on 28 October, setting the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%. The decision was forward-looking. In September, inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% and core measures were still close to 2%. What moved Governing Council was the length of time firms had faced higher costs and the evidence that more of those costs could reach customers. World energy prices and refinery margins remained elevated eight months into the Middle East conflict. Canadian surveys suggested businesses that had largely absorbed the shock expected to pass on more of it over the coming year. Council acted to reduce the risk of that process making inflation persistent and allowed for further increases, while signalling care over subsequent decisions.

The revision was large at the horizon relevant for policy. CPI inflation had been around 3% since April. The Bank now expected about 3½% at year-end and an average of 3% in 2027, a full percentage point above the July projection for that year. It expected a return to 2% in the middle of 2028. The level of gasoline prices explains much of the recent headline overshoot. A persistent rise in production and transportation costs can delay the return to target even after gasoline stops rising, because different sectors revise prices at different times. Imported industrial and electronics inputs had also become more expensive. Near-term household and business inflation expectations had increased, though long-term expectations remained anchored. Governing Council could therefore make a case for insurance against future spread without claiming that broad inflation or long-run expectations had already broken away.

Activity gave the Bank more room to act. GDP rose 3.3% in the second quarter and available indicators suggested about 2% in the third, stronger than the Bank had expected in July. Consumption had been solid despite slow population growth. Investment rebounded in oil and gas and in machinery and equipment. Exports strengthened overall as US demand remained robust, energy production rose and some businesses adapted to the trade environment, even as tariff-exposed sectors struggled. Unemployment had stayed around 6½% for several months, and a broader set of indicators still signalled some spare capacity. Stronger aggregate growth and ongoing slack could coexist, as could gains for energy producers and a cost squeeze for energy users. Those distinctions help explain why Council opted for a limited increase and retained conditional language about the next step.

The growth forecast also had a dip before the recovery. New US tariffs were expected to slow Canadian growth in the fourth quarter. The Bank projected growth of 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028, with business investment, exports and fiscal measures supporting a rebound. Consumption growth was expected to moderate and housing to remain relatively weak. Taken together, that mix means a policy increase could affect borrowers with housing or consumer exposure differently from firms supported by foreign demand or public spending. The statement did not quantify those sensitivities. Canada–US trade relations remained a substantial source of projection uncertainty.

Global news made a simple domestic reading of asset prices especially difficult. The Bank revised 2026 world growth up to 3.1% and projected 3.2% for both following years. Advanced-economy government yields were higher than in July. Equities and credit markets had been volatile amid uncertainty about AI prospects, and the Canadian dollar had recovered to around US$0.71 after an earlier decline. Those observations precede the release. The 25 basis point increase is the observed policy action; its surprise depends on the probability of a rise embedded immediately beforehand. The more distinctive potential signal for markets was the combination of the sizeable inflation forecast revision and Council’s willingness to tighten again if pass-through developed, balanced against acknowledged slack and trade risk. The release provides no trade or quote with which to measure how investors weighted these signals.

questions.question: Did firms’ stated intention to pass through costs turn into broad, sustained price increases?
questions.detail: Match survey intentions to subsequent producer and consumer prices across sectors with differing fuel, transport and imported-input exposure. Separate the timing of contract repricing from new cost shocks and monitor margin changes alongside prices. If the largest increases remain concentrated in fuel, the evidence for the mechanism behind the 2027 forecast revision would be weaker.

questions.question: How much new information did the hike and the revised inflation path convey to markets?
questions.detail: Compare pre-release probabilities or meeting-sensitive overnight-indexed rates with the immediate change in short rates and later forwards. The rate decision and October forecast arrived together, so allow for information about growth and persistence as well as the 25 basis point action. Check for contemporaneous global bond, oil or trade news before attributing a currency or yield movement to domestic policy.

questions.question: Could sectoral slack restrain prices even with stronger aggregate GDP?
questions.detail: Follow orders, employment, wages and capacity utilisation in tariff-exposed manufacturers, oil producers and domestic services, with attention to weaker housing and prospective consumption moderation. Strong energy exports can lift aggregate output while spare capacity persists elsewhere. The sector mix matters for how quickly firms facing higher costs can actually raise prices without losing sales.
